title: Versova-Bandra Sea Link Completes Mumbai's Western Coastal Route
description: The 17.17 km link, whose main span is a 9.8 km eight-lane bridge over the Arabian Sea with four connectors at Bandra, Carter Road, Juhu and Versova, carries the coastal road north from the Bandra-Worli Sea Link to Versova. About 30 per cent of the work was done by early 2026 and the cost has been revised twice, to 18,120.96 crore rupees in 2024.
longFormSummary:
• Seventeen years after it was first planned, the Bandra-Versova sea link - the northwards extension of Mumbai's coastal road - is taking shape but "the pace has been very slow", with work "just about 30 percent complete"; the Fadnavis government is pushing for full completion by 2028, "a deadline that has already been revised several times"
  • Maharashtra CM Devendra Fadnavis directed the contractor to accelerate by deploying more manpower and machinery, and barges were increased from ten to 12, MSRDC officials told the reporter
  • The sea-link "includes a 9.8-km bridge over the sea and four connectors at Bandra, Carter Road, Juhu and Versova, taking the total road length under the project to 17.17 km"
  • The link is expected to cut Bandra-Versova travel time from 45 minutes to roughly 10-15 minutes and to connect south Mumbai to the northwestern suburbs via the coastal road and the Bandra Worli sea link
  • A casting-yard loss is expected to slow it further: of the project's two yards, at Malad and Bandra, "the Bandra one has to be vacated as it is part of the land parcel given to Adani Realty for development", from 24 acres near Mahim Bay that MSRDC monetised, with Adani Realty the preferred bidder promising a 22.79 percent revenue share; working from Malad alone will slow casting and complicate transport, which is feasible only at night
  • Only 3,000 of the 14,000 pre-cast segments that form the viaduct atop the piers have been cast, and only about 40 percent of foundation work is done, with 1,200 of 3,000 piles drilled and installed and a similar share of piers erected
  • Monsoon stops work outright: "Working inside the sea on the already choppy western coast means that we cannot construct anything during the monsoon. From June to the end of September, there is not much scope for work"; construction uses jacked-up barges and reverse circulation drilling machines
  • The cost history is a rise from Rs 7,502 crore estimated in 2017, when the Fadnavis government made it an EPC contract with MSRDC as nodal agency, to Rs 11,332.8 crore on bids in 2018, to Rs 18,120.96 crore in 2024 - two revisions from the original estimate
  • Earlier history: first planned in 2009 on a public-private partnership model with a detailed plan approved by the Congress-NCP cabinet committee on infrastructure in 2011, which did not take off; MSRDC finalised a Reliance Infrastructure-Astaldi joint venture as contractor in 2019 and construction started in 2020, hit by a covid-related slowdown; MSRDC issued a slow-progress notice in 2021 when the deadline stood at 2025; and in January 2022 Reliance Infrastructure exited, transferring its stake to Apco Infratech
  • The project was also delayed by objections from the fishing community over livelihoods, after which the state set up a panel and the project underwent significant design changes

delayReasoning: Stated: the MSRDC contract signed on 4 September 2018 set "a deadline of 24 June 2023 ... for completing the project" (English Wikipedia), while ThePrint reported in February 2026 that the state government "is pushing for the project to be fully complete by 2028, a deadline that has already been revised several times".

title: First Buildings Open at Tokyo's Tsukiji Redevelopment Site

longFormSummary:

  • The scheme covers approximately 190,000 m² of TMG-owned land with a total floor area of about 1,170,000 m² across nine main buildings, at a total expected project cost of approximately ¥900 billion
  • The schedule is given as "first half of 2030s or later (advance opening of facility in fiscal 2029)", so the 2029 date is an advance opening rather than the completion of the scheme
  • The centrepiece is a grand-scale multifunctional venue for about 50,000 people, with seating adjustable from 20,000 to 57,000 and movable and temporary seating to form a stadium, arena, theater or exhibition space for rugby, baseball, soccer, basketball, e-sports, MICE, live music, concerts and theatrical performances, plus one of Japan's largest lounges, VIP rooms, permanent wheelchair seating, audio and text services, a sensory room and a cool down room
  • The other buildings are a life science and commercial complex drawing on proximity to the National Cancer Center Japan, a MICE, hotel and residence building, a boat transport and theater hall complex holding a food hall, a food lab, a roughly 1,200-seat theater hall and a boat waiting area, two further world-class hotels facing Hama-rikyu Gardens, a residence for global executives, an office and residence building, and an office building with shared offices and retail
  • Mitsui Fudosan is representative company alongside Toyota Fudosan and The Yomiuri Shimbun Holdings as operating companies, with Kajima, Shimizu, Taisei and Takenaka building, Nikken Sekkei and Pacific Consultants as architects, and The Asahi Shimbun and Toyota Motor as partners
  • The project is pitched around three roles - "wellness innovation", "food, experience, and activity" and "hospitality" - aimed at a society of healthy longevity and at bolstering Tokyo's international competitiveness while carrying on Japan's food, culture and arts and drawing on Tsukiji's history
  • About 10 hectares of open space will link the site to surrounding resources such as Hama-rikyu Gardens and the Sumida River, with collaboration promised with the Tsukiji outer market
  • Transport plans include a new station on the Rinkai Subway Line linking Tokyo Station and the Rinkai area, a connection to the Metropolitan Expressway's Harumi Route, a port "looking to practical use of flying cars", a Sumida River boat transport hub for tourist and commuter services, and a terminal for buses, taxis and next-generation mobility
  • Carbon neutrality measures listed are wind paths, solar generation, greenery at around a 40% green space ratio, a hydrogen power station and biogas generation
  • Mitsui Fudosan notes the release "presents a summary of the proposal submitted to the Tokyo Metropolitan Government at the present time, and the information is subject to change in the future"

title: The Houston Ship Channel's Project 11 Widening Finishes
description: Project 11 widens the channel by 170 feet along its Galveston Bay reach, from 530 to 700 feet, and deepens upstream segments to 46.5 feet so the largest container ships can pass one another. Dredging began in 2022; Port Houston finished its own segments in October 2025 and the US Army Corps of Engineers is completing the rest, with the spoil building bird islands, marsh and oyster reef.
longFormSummary:
• Project 11, the Houston Ship Channel expansion, "is widening the channel by 170 feet along its Galveston Bay reach, from 530 feet to 700 feet and deepening some upstream segments to 46.5 feet, alongside other safety and efficiency improvements, and crafting new environmental features"
  • Port Houston is the local sponsor, partnering with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers on the federal waterway
  • Dredging began in 2022 and the partners are "expediting the process to complete the work in 2029"; the Corps "will lead the remaining portions of the project, which are scheduled to be completed in 2029"
  • On 27 October 2025 Port Houston announced it had completed its own portion: "the project has reached its most important milestone dredging completion of the widening of the Galveston Bay reach from Bolivar Roads to Morgans Point. With this work done, Port Houston-led project dredging of the Houston Ship Channel is complete"
  • Work still outstanding at that point was the beneficial-use element - "some beneficial use aspects of the project remain under construction, including marsh areas that are being built with dredged material"
  • The scheme is divided into segments: Bolivar Roads to Redfish (about 11.5 miles, widened to 700 feet with bend easings), Redfish to Bayport (about 8.3 miles) and Bayport to Barbours Cut (about 5 miles), both of which are "currently not in the proposed federal plan, so must be built by local interests", plus widening of the Bayport and Barbours Cut ship channels to about 455 feet
  • Upstream, Boggy Bayou (BW 8) to Sims Bayou is widened to about 530 feet and deepened from 41 to 46.5 feet as far as Hunting Bayou, Sims Bayou to IH 610 is deepened from 37 to 41.5 feet, and IH 610 to the Turning Basin from 39 to a potential 41.5 feet with an enlarged Brady Island Turning Basin
  • The two links give different figures for the environmental features, because one states the whole project's plan and the other what the Galveston Bay dredging actually built: the overview promises up to 800 acres of marsh across three new marshes, bird islands "up to 20 acres in total" and "approximately 375 acres" of new oyster reef substrate, while the completion release says the Galveston Bay features "will ultimately include approximately 10 acres of bird islands, 276 acres of marsh, and 324 acres of oyster reefs"
  • The bird islands are supported by the Beneficial Use Group, which includes Port Houston and state and federal environmental agencies, and one triangular marsh "will have a bird island at each corner"
  • Air quality gains are claimed both ways: the expansion "is expected to improve regional air quality by reducing ship emissions... through more efficient vessel movements and avoiding congestion", with vessel nitrogen oxide emissions "expected to be reduced by between three percent and seven percent" and dredges on the first three segments fitted with Tier 3 or Tier 4 engines or scrubbers
  • The widening is aimed at the "Texas Chicken" maneuver, "unique to the Houston Ship Channel", in which ships from opposing directions "meet each other head-on but still safely pass each other, as hydrodynamic forces keep the vessels from touching", a manoeuvre "necessary in relatively narrow channels like ours"
  • The navigation payoff is already visible: the Houston Pilots revised their Navigation Safety Guidelines so that "daylight restricted vessels now have up to an additional two and a half hours to transit into and out of port each day", and earlier phases let vessels "between 15,000 and 17,000 TEU - matching the capacity of the Panama Canal" call at Bayport Container Terminal
  • Planning began in 2010; the Corps finished its five-year Houston Ship Channel Mega Study, the Chief of Engineers signed the final Chief's Report in April 2020, the project was authorized in the Water Resources and Development Act of 2020, and on 19 January 2021 it received a "new start" designation with $19.5 million in federal funds
  • The two links size the channel's economy differently: the overview claims "$987 billion in annual national economic value" and "more than three million U.S. jobs", while the completion release cites a 2022 third-party study giving "3.37 million jobs nationwide and ... $906 billion in annual economic activity", the newer and sourced of the two figures
  • The Corps recognised the 52-mile channel as the busiest waterway in the United States, "handling approximately 12% of the nation's total waterborne tonnage", serving more than 200 private facilities and eight public terminals; a draft Perryman Group study estimates Segment 1 alone will generate $60.95 billion in statewide benefit and 440,665 Texas jobs by 2040
  • The project won the 2025 Western Dredging Association Environmental Excellence Award and the 2025 Texas ASCE Outstanding Civil Engineering Achievement Award
address: Houston Ship Channel, Galveston Bay reach near Morgans Point, Texas
dateConfidenceReasoning: Port Houston's project page describes "expediting the process to complete the work in 2029", a year rather than a day, so it sits at the end of that year.

references.title: Port Houston Completes its Portion of Project 11 Dredging (27 October 2025)
references.reasoning: Port Houston’s own release dating the halfway mark this pin’s description rests on: "Port Houston-led project dredging of the Houston Ship Channel is complete", with the Galveston Bay reach widened from 530 to 700 feet, while "some beneficial use aspects of the project remain under construction". The 2029 date is for the whole of Project 11, not this portion.

title: Vadhavan Port's First Phase Opens on Maharashtra's Coast

  • It is developed by Vadhavan Port Project Limited, an SPV of the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority and the Maharashtra Maritime Board holding 74 per cent and 26 per cent, working on a landlord model in which the SPV builds breakwaters, rail and road links, power, water and common services

  • Planned facilities: nine container terminals of 1,000 metres each, four multipurpose berths including the coastal berth, four liquid cargo berths, a Ro-Ro berth and a Coast Guard berth
  • The works involve reclaiming 1,448 hectares of sea and building 10.14 km of offshore breakwater plus container and cargo storage areas
  • Shore protection projects worth Rs 1,700 crore have already been awarded
  • The pin's 20 m draft and 233,000 DWT ship capability, and its 30 August 2024 groundbreaking, are not stated in the source

title: New Ontario Science Centre Opens at Ontario Place
description: The 400,000-square-foot replacement for the Don Mills science centre is rising on Toronto's waterfront, pairing a mainland building with an integrated pod complex and a restored Cinesphere. Ontario's auditor general costed the move at roughly $1.4 billion against $1.3 billion to keep the old building, and shovels went in the ground in May 2026.
longFormSummary:
• Infrastructure officials told the auditor general's office that the new Ontario Science Centre at Ontario Place "is expected to be up and running in 2029", and auditor general Shelley Spence's report on the Ontario Place redevelopment says "the new building is expected to open in 2029", information her spokesperson attributed to Infrastructure Ontario
  • That is a slip from the government's own earlier dates: when Premier Doug Ford announced the move from the science centre's east Toronto location, "the science centre said the new facility would open in 2028", and in June, announcing the abrupt closure of the old building over structural concerns with the roof, the government's press release said the Ontario Place facility would open "as early as" 2028
  • On costs, the audit found it will now cost more to build the new centre than to maintain the closed site: the estimate for building and maintaining a new science centre at Ontario Place "has increased by nearly $400 million from the government's spring 2023 business case", to approximately $1.4 billion, "higher than the $1.3-billion estimate for maintaining the attraction at its east Toronto location"
  • Spence attributed the increase to higher design and construction costs, life cycle and maintenance costs, and ancillary costs from scope changes plus about $61 million in cost escalations
  • Michael Lindsay, then president and CEO of Infrastructure Ontario, disputed the comparison, noting that rehabilitating the old building would also face inflationary increases, and said the "as early as" 2028 wording "probably just reflects the realities of procurement and construction"
  • Procurement was continuing "with the request for proposals stage expected to wrap up next fall"; Infrastructure Ontario's Karen Evans said a firm construction completion date would be posted once a contract is awarded and the opening date depends on the move-in timeline - "The overall plan for delivering the vision remains unchanged"
  • An interim centre is planned but had gone without public updates since a June RFP seeking about 50,000 to 100,000 square feet of retail or commercial space - "much smaller than the original building's 568,000 square feet" - with a start date of "no later than" Jan. 1, 2026 and a lease of up to five years plus three one-year extensions, which Jason Ash said would allow a temporary science centre until 2034; meanwhile the centre runs pop-up exhibits at Harbourfront Centre and Sherway Gardens mall
  • Jason Ash of Save Ontario's Science Centre: "It's really a whole generation of Ontario children who are not going to have access to world-class science education that the Ontario Science Centre has provided for 55 years"
  • The political backdrop: NDP Leader Marit Stiles' integrity complaint of October 16th, 2024 focused largely on the 95-year lease for Therme to build and operate a spa and waterpark at Ontario Place but also alleges "irregularities" with the science centre relocation, and Infrastructure Minister Kinga Surma was asked not to comment because of it; Stiles said "Ford and Surma boasted about the new Science Centre opening in 2028, but that sounds like more false promises from a flailing government"
  • The wiki does not carry the pin's building details - the 400,000 square feet, the mainland building with an integrated pod complex, the restored Cinesphere, or a May 2026 construction start
address: Ontario Place, 955 Lake Shore Boulevard West, Toronto, Ontario, Canada
dateConfidenceReasoning: Global News reports that "the new building is expected to open in 2029", a year rather than a fixed day, so the pin sits at the end of 2029.
delayReasoning: Stated: the province had said "the Ontario Place facility would open 'as early as' 2028", but infrastructure officials told the auditor general that "the new building is expected to open in 2029".

title: Naval architect says 3D printing entire superyachts will be a reality by 2030

title: Annular Solar Eclipse Crosses Russia
description: The Moon's shadow touches down at 06:27:55 UT on 2030-06-01, and the annular phase lasts up to 5 minutes 21 seconds along a path 249.6 km wide crossing Algeria, Tunisia, Greece, Turkey, Russia, n. longFormSummary:
• An annular solar eclipse on 2030 Jun 01, its antumbral shadow path computed by Fred Espenak for NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center
  • Greatest eclipse falls at 06:27:55.6 UT at 56°31.5'N, 080°04.5'E in Russia, with the Sun 55.5° up, a path 249.6 km wide and a central-line duration of 05m20.8s
  • Greatest duration is only 43 seconds later and barely east of it, at 06:28:38 UT at 56°33'N, 080°31'E, with the same 249.6 km width and the same 05m20.8s; the Google map page repeats the figure, "In this case, the Greatest Duration is 05m20.8s"
  • The saros catalogue lists the same eclipse as 2030 Jun 01 at 06:29:13 TD (Terrestrial Dynamical Time, against the path table's Universal Time) at 56.5°N 80.1°E, path width 250 km and central duration 05m21s
  • The path table gives 98 timed rows at 120-second intervals from 04:50 UT to 08:04 UT, plus opening and closing "Limits" rows, in WGS 84 coordinates
  • The central line enters at 04:50 UT near 29°42.6'N, 004°23.2'E in Algeria and leaves at 08:04 UT near 37°52.6'N, 154°07.2'E in the north-west Pacific beyond Japan; the outer limit rows run from 29°26.4'N, 003°44.7'E to 33°41.6'N, 163°41.5'E
  • At the ends of the track the path is much wider and annularity shorter - about 344-345 km and 04m12-04m13s at the limit rows - against 249.6 km and 05m20.8s at greatest eclipse
  • The eclipse is member 16 of Saros 128 (sequence number 09575), with gamma 0.5626 and eclipse magnitude 0.9443
  • Saros 128 runs 1298.17 years from a partial eclipse on 0984 Aug 29 to a partial eclipse on 2282 Nov 01, occurs at the Moon's descending node and holds 73 eclipses in the sequence 24P 4T 4H 32A 9P; its longest annular was 1832 Feb 01 at 08m35s, so this one is well short of the series maximum
  • Predictions use the VSOP87/ELP2000-85 solar and lunar ephemerides with ΔT = 76.9 seconds; the catalogue row carries ΔT = 78 s
  • Annularity is visible only inside the central path between the blue limit lines on the map and is longest on the central line, with a green GE marker at greatest eclipse and a magenta GD marker at greatest duration
  • The predictions "DO NOT include the effects of mountains and valleys along the edge of the Moon"; limb corrections may shift the path limits north or south by ~1-3 km and change durations by ~1-3 seconds, and more detailed predictions "are normally posted 12-18 months before each eclipse"

title: Total Solar Eclipse Crosses Botswana
description: The Moon's shadow touches down at 06:50:19 UT on 2030-11-25, and the total phase lasts up to 3 minutes 44 seconds along a path 169.3 km wide crossing Botswana, S. Africa and Australia. A partial eclipse is visible from southern Africa, southern Indian Oc., the East Indies, Australia and Antarctica.
longFormSummary:
• A total solar eclipse on 2030 Nov 25, catalogued by NASA/GSFC as sequence 09576, relative number 10, of Saros series 133
  • Greatest Eclipse falls at 06:50:19.2 UT at 43°36.8'S 071°14.5'E, with the Sun 67.0° up, a path 169.3 km wide and a central duration of 03m43.5s
  • Greatest Duration comes a little later, at 06:51:53 UT at 43°43'S 072°02'E, path width 169.2 km, central duration 03m43.6s, the figure the Google-map page also gives: ‘In this case, the Greatest Duration is 03m43.6s’
  • The umbral shadow is tabulated at 120-second intervals across 95 timed rows from 05:16 UT to 08:24 UT, the central line running from 16°13.0'S 001°36.5'E at the opening limits to 26°20.6'S 151°11.7'E at the closing limits
  • At the path’s ends totality is far shorter — 01m30.8s over a 117 km path at the start and 01m32.1s over 118 km at the end — against 03m43.5s at greatest eclipse
  • The Saros 133 catalog gives the same instant in Terrestrial Dynamical Time as 2030 Nov 25 06:51:37 TD with ΔT = 78 s, gamma -0.3867, magnitude 1.0468, path width 169 km and central duration 03m44s — rounded against the path page’s 169.3 km and 03m43.5s
  • Totality can only be seen between the blue northern and southern path limits and is longest on the red central line; yellow lines mark maximum eclipse at 10-minute intervals
  • Predictions use the VSOP87/ELP2000-85 solar and lunar ephemerides with ΔT = 77.3 seconds, and exclude the lunar limb profile, whose corrections ‘may shift the limits of the eclipse path north or south by ~1-3 kilometers, and change the eclipse duration by ~1-3 seconds’
  • Saros 133 runs 1280.14 years over 72 solar eclipses, 46 of them total, from a partial on 1219 Jul 13 to a partial on 2499 Sep 05; this eclipse follows 2012 Nov 13 (04m02s) and precedes 2048 Dec 05 (03m28s) as the series’ durations shorten
  • All calculations are by Fred Espenak, NASA’s GSFC, who ‘assumes full responsibility for their accuracy’
address: Point of greatest eclipse at sea, off Botswana
dateConfidenceReasoning: NASA's eclipse catalogue gives the instant of greatest eclipse as 06:50:19 UT on 2030-11-25 (06:51:37 TD, the two separated by delta-T), from Saros series 133. Eclipse circumstances are computed from orbital mechanics, so the date and time are exact centuries ahead.

title: Eglinton Crosstown West Extension Opens to Renforth
description: The 9.2-kilometre westward extension of Line 5 Eglinton adds seven stations - four underground, two elevated and one in an open trench - ending at a trenched terminal at Renforth beside the eastern end of the Mississauga Transitway. Construction was estimated in 2026 at CA$3.97 billion, up from CA$2.47 billion a decade earlier.
longFormSummary:
• The Eglinton Crosstown west extension carries Toronto's Line 5 Eglinton 9.2 km (6 mi) west from Mount Dennis station to a new Renforth station in Mississauga, and “is expected to open in 2031” — the only opening timing the article gives, with no month or day
  • It adds seven stations: Jane and Scarlett elevated, Royal York, Islington, Kipling and Martin Grove underground, and Renforth in an open trench
  • West of Mount Dennis a short tunnel leads to a 1.5 km elevated structure over the Humber River, then a 6.3 km tunnel carries the four underground through-stations, ending at Renforth on the north side of the existing bus rapid transit station at the eastern terminus of the Mississauga Transitway, with connections to MiWay and GO buses
  • Renforth is the extension's only station in Mississauga; five of the stations carry temporary working names that clash with existing Line 2 and Line 6 stations and will be renamed after surrounding neighbourhoods
  • The cost is stated several ways across the article's planning history: CA$2.47 billion for the surface Eglinton West LRT in June 2016; $1.5–2.1 billion fully at grade in 2017, with grade separation adding $881.9 million to $1.32 billion; “expected to cost $4.7 billion” for the mostly grade-separated option against $2.9 billion for a surface line in the 2020 business case; and CA$3.97 billion as estimated in 2026
  • The ridership figures also disagree: the project is “forecast to serve 96,700 daily riders”, while the 2020 comparison gave the grade-separated seven-station line an estimated 37,000 daily boardings against 42,500 for a ten-stop surface line
  • Metrolinx owns the extension and the Toronto Transit Commission will operate it
  • Ontario premier Doug Ford announced the grade-separated extension in April 2019; Metrolinx settled on the mostly grade-separated seven-station design after a February 2020 business case, with an updated environmental assessment finalised in June 2020
  • Preliminary construction began in 2020, and on 20 May 2021 the design-build-finance tunnelling contract went to West End Connectors, a consortium of Dragados, Aecon and Ghella, for 6 km of tunnels between Renforth Drive and Scarlett Road
  • Tunnelling began on 11 April 2022 from a launch shaft beside Renforth Transitway station using two TBMs, Rexy and Renny, each about 750 tonnes, 6.58 m in diameter and 131 m long — longer than those used on the central section — boring 20 m down; Renny broke through near Scarlett Road in May 2024 and Rexy three weeks later
  • Aecon won the 1.5 km elevated guideway contract on 15 December 2023, and Strabag won the second advance tunnel (500 m from east of Jane Street to Mount Dennis) on 16 February 2024, with sequential-excavation construction starting in February 2025
  • The stations, rail and systems contract, covering all seven stations, 9.2 km of track, signalling, electrification and commissioning, went to RFP on 27 September 2024 among three consortia, with a two-year design development phase anticipated to have begun in mid-2025
  • The underground stations are being built by cut-and-cover because they are comparatively shallow and Eglinton Avenue's right-of-way is wide there, having originally been reserved for the Richview Expressway
  • A coalition of community and local First Nations groups opposed the elevated Humber River crossing from 2022, protesting in 2023; Metrolinx defended the elevated route on flooding grounds, citing Hurricane Hazel in 1954 and 2013, and the coalition's 2024 injunction attempt was rejected in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice
  • Metrolinx has proposed extending the line further north from Renforth to Toronto Pearson International Airport, with intermediate stations at Convair and Silver Dart, but as of March 2024 that route had not been finalised

title: BART's Silicon Valley Extension Reaches Downtown San Jose and Santa Clara
description: VTA's Phase II extension carries BART on from Berryessa through a five-mile single-bore tunnel to three new subway stations in San Jose - 28th Street/Little Portugal, Downtown San Jose and Diridon - plus a surface station at Santa Clara. Excavation of the tunnel boring machine entrance pit at Newhall Yard was in progress in late 2025.
longFormSummary:
• BART Silicon Valley Phase II carries the line 6 miles (9.7 km) on from Berryessa to Santa Clara, largely underground, adding subway stations at 28th Street/Little Portugal, Downtown San José and Diridon plus a surface station at Santa Clara
  • The article dates completion two ways: the phases table and infobox give a planned opening of 2037 and the text says it is “targeted for completion in 2037”, while the route map marks the four new stations as 2036
  • The cost is also stated two ways in the same article: “the $12.7 billion third phase” in the phases table and overview, against “an estimated cost of $6.8 billion” for the final Downtown San Jose/Santa Clara leg
  • Funding is not fully finalised: VTA is counting on a 2016 half-cent sales tax worth up to $1.6 billion for BART, $2.6 billion awarded from the state's Transit and Intercity Rail Capital Program in 2018, $125 million from the FTA in August 2019 and an FTA commitment of $5 billion made in August 2024, and plans to apply for a Full Funding Grant Agreement after covering existing funding gaps
  • Initial testing and preliminary construction began in January 2019, groundbreaking was on 14 June 2024, and excavation of the tunnel boring machine entrance pit was in progress as of late 2025 — the infobox places that pit excavation and TBM testing at the Santa Clara station site
  • The route runs south from Berryessa into a tunnel crossing the Bayshore Freeway to 28th Street/Little Portugal, west under Santa Clara Street to a Downtown San Jose station interchanging with VTA light rail, on underground to San Jose Diridon (a transfer to Amtrak, Caltrain, ACE, VTA light rail and bus and the planned California High-Speed Rail), then surfaces at the current Santa Clara Caltrain Station site
  • The tunnel's length is given inconsistently: the phase is described as “featuring a 5-mile-long (8.0 km) tunnel”, while the contract awarded to Kiewit Shea Traylor Joint Venture in May 2022 was to “bore the 4-mile tunnel from Berryessa to Diridon” and build the 1-mile above-ground stretch on to Santa Clara
  • The tunnel is a single bore after a late-2017 dispute in which VTA favoured one 45-foot-wide bore configured as a double-deck stack and BART preferred two horizontally separated 20-foot bores; the two agreed on the single bore the following March, and the $125 million engineering contract went to a Mott MacDonald and PGH Wong Engineering joint venture
  • The original proposal had additional subway stations at Civic Plaza/SJSU and Plaza de César Chávez between Alum Rock and downtown, consolidated into a single station to cut costs
  • A 40-acre BART maintenance yard at Newhall, on land VTA bought from Union Pacific just south of Santa Clara station, is part of this phase; like the Berryessa extension it would be built by VTA and operated by BART
  • The opening has slipped repeatedly: in September 2019 the project was delayed three to four years with revenue service to begin in 2029–2030, in October 2023 it was pushed to 2036, and in June 2025 agency staff recommended terminating the Kiewit Shea Traylor contract over an unresolved cost disagreement, a change estimated to add 18 months of delay
  • The phase follows the $2.3 billion Berryessa extension, which opened to the public on 13 June 2020, and the $790 million Warm Springs extension of March 2017
  • The article carries a maintenance banner saying it needs to be updated, dated August 2023

title: Total Solar Eclipse Crosses Australia
description: The Moon's shadow touches down at 02:39:13 UT on 2037-07-13, and the total phase lasts up to 3 minutes 58 seconds along a path 200.7 km wide crossing Australia and New Zealand. A partial eclipse is visible from the East Indies, Australia and the Pacific.
longFormSummary:
• NASA/GSFC (Fred Espenak) predicts a total solar eclipse on 2037 Jul 13, with greatest eclipse at 02:39:13.3 UT at latitude 24°46.1'S, longitude 139°04.5'E
  • At that point the path is 200.7 km wide, the central-line duration is 03m58.4s and the Sun stands 43.4° above the horizon at azimuth 3.3°
  • Greatest duration comes moments later, at 02:39:41 UT at 24°47'S 139°14'E, with the same 03m58.4s over a 200.6 km path; the interactive map page gives the same figure, "In this case, the Greatest Duration is 03m58.4s"
  • The Saros catalogue lists the same eclipse with its time in Terrestrial Dynamical Time rather than UT - "2037 Jul 13 02:40:36 TD" - and rounds the figures to a 201 km path and 03m58s of totality, magnitude 1.0413, gamma -0.7246, at 24.8S 139.1E with the Sun at 43 degrees; the dedicated path page's 02:39:13.3 UT and 200.7 km are the more precise statement of the same instant
  • The umbral track begins and ends over water at sunrise and sunset geometry: the opening "Limits" row has the central line at 39°42.5'S 089°17.6'E with the Sun on the horizon, a 124 km path and 01m49.6s of totality, and the closing row at 45°17.9'S 170°24.3'W with a 128 km path and 01m53.2s
  • Totality is only visible from inside the central path: the page states a viewer "MUST be somewhere within the central path (between the blue lines) to see the total phase of the eclipse", and the eclipse is longest on the central line
  • The eclipse belongs to Saros 127, an unusual series of 82 solar eclipses running 0991 Oct 10 to 2452 Mar 21 (1460.44 years) made up only of partial and total eclipses - 40 partial and 42 total, with no annular or hybrid members - all at the Moon's ascending node
  • Within that series the 2037 eclipse sits in the declining half, between 2019 Jul 02 (04m33s) and 2055 Jul 24 (03m17s), against the series' longest total of 05m40s on 1532 Aug 30 and its shortest of 01m38s on 2091 Aug 15
  • Predictions were generated using the VSOP87/ELP2000-85 solar and lunar ephemerides and a value of ΔT = 81.9 seconds
  • The predictions "DO NOT include the effects of mountains and valleys along the edge of the Moon"; lunar limb corrections "may shift the limits of the eclipse path north or south by ~1-3 kilometers, and change the eclipse duration by ~1-3 seconds", and "The exact location of Greatest Duration may also change by ~10-20 kilometers"
  • More detailed predictions including the lunar limb profile "are normally posted 12-18 months before each eclipse"
  • The path is tabulated at 120-second intervals in WGS 84 coordinates for the northern limit, southern limit and central line, with the diameter ratio, Sun altitude and azimuth, path width and central duration for each row
  • Neither page carries a labelled publication date; the Google map page ends with the bare stamp "2014 Mar 14" and the Saros catalogue with "2009 Sep 26"

title: New York Harbor Storm Surge Plan
description: The US Army Corps of Engineers is advancing a $52.6BN plan of storm-surge gates, sea walls and levees around New York Harbor, after shelving a more radical $119BN 'mega sea wall' spanning the harbor mouth.
longFormSummary:
• The Army Corps' NY & NJ Harbor & Tributaries Focus Area Feasibility Study (HATS), begun after Hurricane Sandy, tentatively selected Alternative 3B in July 2022 at about $52 billion
  • The plan has 12 storm surge gates and coastal barriers across more than 41 miles of shoreline, with 14 years of construction; final designs were anticipated from 2025 and construction from 2030
  • Largest gates are on the Arthur Kill and Kill Van Kull and at the entrance to Jamaica Bay; onshore defences include seawalls and floodwalls in East Harlem, Lower Manhattan, southern Brooklyn and the Rockaways
  • It could cut coastal-storm damages from 2044 to 2093 by an average of $6.2 billion a year, but the gates do not address sea level rise or rainfall flooding such as Hurricane Ida
  • The largest alternative, a $119 billion five-mile barrier from Sandy Hook to Breezy Point, was mocked by Trump, study funding halted in February 2020 and restarted in October 2021
  • Riverkeeper called HATS "fatally flawed" and other groups raised habitat and trapped-runoff concerns; Jamaica Bay is expected to see the largest environmental impact
address: Rockaway Beach, Queens, New York, USA
dateConfidenceReasoning: A target, per the source: if approved, "work would begin in 2030 and be completed by 2044"; as of now the plan "has not yet received final approval."

  • The central phase is longest at the sunrise end of the track: the point of Greatest Duration is 03:49:13 UT at 21°02'N 037°51'E, with the Sun on the horizon (altitude 0.0°), a path 40.0 km wide and a central duration of 00m41.8s
  • The central path crosses Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Malaysia and Indonesia, while the partial eclipse is visible from eastern Africa, southern Asia, the East Indies and Australia

title: World population projected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050
description: The current world population of 7.3 billion is expected to reach 8.5 billion by 2030, 9.7 billion in 2050 and 11.2 billion in 2100, according to a new UN DESA report, “World Population Prospects: The 2015 Revision”, launched today. longFormSummary:
• The UN projects world population rising from about 7.7 billion (2019 estimate) to 9.7 billion in 2050, possibly peaking near 11 billion late in the century, though the UN's Population Division director says that peak "is not certain"
  • More than half of the growth to 2050 comes from nine countries: India, Nigeria, Pakistan, DR Congo, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Indonesia, Egypt and the United States; sub-Saharan Africa's population nearly doubles
  • India is projected to overtake China (by 2027 in the 2019 revision), while China's population falls by more than two percent by 2050
  • Fertility fell from 3.2 births per woman in 1990 to 2.5 in 2019 and is projected at 2.2 by 2050, against 2.1 needed for replacement
  • 27 countries or areas lost at least one percent of population since 2010; 55 countries are projected to shrink by 1% or more by 2050
  • Life expectancy is expected to reach 77.1 years in 2050, up from 72.6 now

title: Hybrid Solar Eclipse Crosses the South Pacific
description: The Moon's shadow touches down at 20:41:15 UT on 2050-05-20, and the hybrid phase lasts up to 0 minutes 21 seconds along a path 26.7 km wide crossing the South Pacific. A partial eclipse is visible from New Zealand., the South Pacific and southwestern South America.
longFormSummary:
• A hybrid solar eclipse on 2050 May 20, its umbral shadow path computed by Fred Espenak for NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center
  • Greatest eclipse falls at 20:41:15.0 UT at 40°05.3'S, 123°42.4'W in the South Pacific, with the Sun only 29.4° up, a path 26.7 km wide and a central-line duration of 00m21.3s
  • Greatest duration comes two minutes earlier, at 20:39:15 UT at 40°15'S, 124°33'W, where the path is 26.6 km wide and the central phase lasts 00m21.4s; the Google map page gives the same figure, "In this case, the Greatest Duration is 00m21.4s"
  • The saros catalogue lists the same eclipse as 2050 May 20 at 20:42:50 TD (Terrestrial Dynamical Time, against the path table's Universal Time) at 40.1°S 123.7°W, path width 27 km and central duration 00m21s
  • The path table runs at 120-second intervals in Universal Time from an opening "Limits" row through 19:48 to 21:34 and a closing "Limits" row
  • Its hybrid character shows in the Moon/Sun diameter ratio, which runs from 0.996 at the start up through 1.000 to a maximum 1.004 in mid-path and back down to 0.995 at the end - annular at the ends, total in the middle
  • At 19:54 UT the central line is at 51°08.7'S, 150°49.3'W with ratio 1.000, a path just 1 km wide and a central duration of 00m00s, the changeover point
  • The longest tabulated central duration is 00m21.4s at 20:40 UT, central line 40°11.0'S, 124°14.3'W, Sun altitude 29°, azimuth 353°, width 27 km
  • The eclipse is member -13 of Saros 148 (sequence number 09619), with gamma -0.8688 and eclipse magnitude 1.0038
  • It is the only hybrid eclipse of Saros 148 - the catalogue lists it as both the longest and the shortest hybrid of the series, at 00m21s
  • Saros 148 runs 1334.23 years from a partial eclipse on 1653 Sep 21 to a partial eclipse on 2987 Dec 12, occurs at the Moon's descending node and holds 75 eclipses in the sequence 20P 2A 1H 40T 12P - 32 partial, 2 annular, 1 hybrid and 40 total
  • Predictions use the VSOP87/ELP2000-85 solar and lunar ephemerides with ΔT = 94.5 seconds; the catalogue row carries ΔT = 94 s
  • Annularity or totality is visible only inside the central path between the blue limit lines on the map and is longest on the central line; the page marks greatest eclipse with a green GE marker and greatest duration with a magenta GD marker

title: Kansai Airport Could Sink Below Sea Level by 2056
description: Built on an artificial island, Japan's Kansai International Airport has sunk more than 13 metres since opening and could drop below sea level by 2056 if its current subsidence rate continues.
longFormSummary:
• Kansai International Airport opened in 1994 on an artificial island in Osaka Bay, at a cost of more than $20 billion
  • It sits on soft alluvial clay; by 1990 it had sunk 27 feet, 50% more than the expected 19 feet, because of underestimated settlement and incomplete consolidation
  • Sinking rates fell from over 19 inches a year at opening to 2.8 inches a year by 2008 and 2.3 inches in 2023 after sand drains, jacking of foundations and $150 million on the seawall
  • Some engineers predict sections could be below sea level as soon as 2056
  • NASA in 2004 noted 2-4 cm a year of subsidence; the terminal by Renzo Piano survived the magnitude 6.7 Kobe earthquake four months after opening
  • In 2024 the airport handled 25.9 million passengers and 169,774 aircraft movements
dateConfidenceReasoning: A target, per the source: "current forecasts predict that Kansai could drop below sea level by 2056 if it continues sinking at the current rate."

title: Halley's Comet Returns to Perihelion
description: The most famous comet swings back through the inner solar system on its 76-year orbit, having last appeared in 1986.
longFormSummary:
• Halley's Comet (1P/Halley) is the only known short-period comet consistently visible to the naked eye; last perihelion 8-9 February 1986, next perihelion 28 July 2061 (then about 27 March 2134)
  • Its period varies between about 74 and 79-80 years; the orbit is retrograde with eccentricity 0.967, perihelion 0.59 au (between Mercury and Venus) and aphelion about 35 au
  • In 1705 Edmond Halley linked the 1531, 1607 and 1682 comets and predicted a 1758 return, confirmed when it was first seen on 25 December 1758; it has been recorded since at least 240 BC
  • In 1986 a fleet including Giotto (ESA), Vega 1 and 2, Suisei and Sakigake observed it, the first comet studied in detail by spacecraft
  • The nucleus is about 15 x 8 x 8 km (mean diameter 11 km), a dark dirty snowball; it sheds an estimated 1 to 3 metres of surface per orbit
  • Space.com's 2023 preview gives inbound crossings (Earth's orbit 19 June 2061, Venus 9 July 2061), naked-eye visibility from mid-June 2061, and the best evening view around 4-8 August 2061, brighter than in 1986

title: Will Humans Achieve a Type 1 Civilization by 2100?
description: Based on Kardashev’s speculations where does our civilization sit today? We are Type 0, somewhere between 0.7 and 0.72 producing 15 Terawatts of energy, a mere fraction of the energy a Type 1 would harvest from the physical world. The renowned theoretical physicist, Michio Kaku, has speculated on Kardashev’s scale and believes humanity will attain Type 1 status within a century or two.
longFormSummary:
• The Kardashev scale rates a civilization by how much energy it can harness, from its home planet (Type I) to its star (Type II) to its galaxy (Type III).
  • Humanity today sits at Type 0, scoring roughly 0.7 to 0.72 and producing about 15 terawatts of energy - a small fraction of a Type I civilization's output.
  • Physicist Michio Kaku has speculated humanity will reach Type I status within a century or two, putting the milestone around 2100-2200.
  • Kaku's own site separately estimates a Type I civilization is roughly 200 years away, consistent with that century-or-two outlook.
dateConfidenceReasoning: No wording about the date available; treat it as unverified.
